Counsel.Lead: Nicola Shaw KC (instructed by Ernst & Young LLP)

SummaryOfPosition.Summary: The Respondent contends that the Borgsten Dolphin should not be classified as a 'relevant asset' under Part 8ZA as any accommodation provided was ancillary to its primary TSV functions and constitutes incidental use within the statutory framework.

FactsReliedOn.item: Dolphin leased the Borgsten Dolphin and supplied it to Total E&P UK for the Dunbar platform.
The Borgsten provided tender‑assisted drilling (TAD) and related TSV services.
Sleeping accommodation was provided for Total personnel (initially around 40 berths, later increased).
The relevant accounting periods were calendar years 2014 and 2015; Part 8ZA CTA 2010 applied with effect from 1 April 2014.

Contentions.item: The Borgsten’s primary function was as a template support vessel (TSV) providing tender‑assisted drilling and related services to the Dunbar platform; accommodation was ancillary to those services.
Any accommodation provided to Total personnel (initially 40 berths, later increased) was functionally connected to the TSV operations and thus no more than incidental within s.356LA(3).

On a proper construction of Part 8ZA, the asset should not be classified as a ‘relevant asset’ merely because it could provide accommodation; the legislative target was accommodation vessels and drilling rigs, not TSVs performing multi‑purpose support tasks.
The First‑tier Tribunal’s factual evaluation should be respected and was correctly upheld by the Upper Tribunal.

LegalBasis.item: Corporation Tax Act 2010, Part 8ZA (Oil Contractors), including ss. 356K (overview), 356L (definitions), 356LA (relevant asset), 356M.
Finance Act 2014, s.73 and Schedule 16 (inserting Part 8ZA into CTA 2010).

ReliefSought.item: Dismiss the appeal and uphold the Upper Tribunal’s decision.
Declare that the Borgsten is not a ‘relevant asset’ in the relevant periods because accommodation use was no more than incidental to its TSV functions.

AuthoritiesCited.Authority: Proctor & Gamble UK v HMRC [2009] EWCA Civ 407

Timeline.Event: Total invited tenders for TAD and accommodation services for the Dunbar project.
Dolphin awarded Letter of Intent indicating intention to engage the Borgsten as a TSV with accommodation.
Contract signed between Total and Dolphin; accommodation initially specified for 40 Total personnel.
Commencement of services under the contract (per case narrative).
Part 8ZA of the CTA 2010 treated as coming into force.
Start of relevant accounting period for 2014.

SourceExtracts.Quote: Dolphin leased an asset called the Borgsten Dolphin (“the Borgsten”) from an associated company in Singapore called Borgsten Dolphin Pte Ltd (“BDPL”), and in turn provided it to Total E&P UK Ltd (“Total”), the operator of the Dunbar oil platform (“the Dunbar”).

The Borgsten had formerly been a drilling rig but was converted so as to be able to provide a number of services in connection with the preparation of the Dunbar for drilling, and then the operation of the Dunbar.
Among other services, the Borgsten was used to provide sleeping accommodation for a number of those who worked on the Dunbar.

On the particular facts that will have been the case unless it was “reasonable to suppose” that the use of the Borgsten as accommodation for those who worked on the Dunbar “is unlikely to be more than incidental to another use, or other uses, to which [the Borgsten] is likely to be put”.
The question whether the hire cap applies to Dolphin’s payments to BDPL depends on whether the Borgsten was a “relevant asset”.

It is common ground that the Dunbar (which lies north-east of the Shetland Islands in the UK sector of the North Sea) is in a relevant offshore area, and that Dolphin provided the Borgsten to Total in connection with the carrying on of exploration or exploitation activities by Dolphin.
So the critical question is whether the Borgsten was a relevant asset.

HMRC v Dolphin Drilling Ltd (ii) provide accommodation for individuals who work on or from another structure used in a relevant offshore area for, or in connection with, exploration or exploitation activities (“offshore workers’’).
